definition: A fast, usually in-memory store holding copies of data that is expensive to fetch or compute, so repeat requests are served quickly.
The fraction of requests answered from the cache; the average latency is hit ratio times cache latency plus miss ratio times backend latency.
A pattern in which the application checks the cache first, loads from the database on a miss, and then writes the result into the cache itself.
A cache that loads missing data from the backing store itself, so the application only ever talks to the cache.
A write strategy in which data is written to the cache and the database synchronously, keeping them consistent at the cost of slower writes.
A write strategy that acknowledges after writing to the cache and flushes to the database later, which is fast but risks losing data if the cache fails.
A write strategy that writes straight to the database and skips the cache, avoiding cache pollution from data that is rarely read.
Proactively reloading a cache entry shortly before it expires so readers rarely hit a cold miss.
The rule a full cache uses to decide which entry to discard, such as LRU, LFU or FIFO.
Least recently used: evict the entry that has gone longest without being accessed, assuming recent use predicts future use.
Least frequently used: evict the entry accessed the fewest times, favoring items that are consistently popular.
First in, first out: evict the oldest inserted entry regardless of how often or recently it was used.
Removing or updating cached entries when the underlying data changes so readers do not see stale values.
Many requests miss the same expired or evicted key at once and all hit the database simultaneously; also called a thundering herd.
Letting only one request rebuild a missing cache entry while concurrent requests for the same key wait and share the result.
A single key that receives far more traffic than others, overloading the one cache or database node that owns it.
Caching the fact that something does not exist so repeated lookups for missing keys do not keep reaching the database.
An in-memory data structure store used as a cache, database and message broker, offering strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets and optional persistence.
A simple, multithreaded, in-memory key-value cache for small objects, with no persistence and no built-in replication.
The identifier under which an entry is stored; in a CDN it is built from the URL plus selected headers, so a wrong key serves the wrong content.
An HTTP validator header identifying a version of a resource, letting clients revalidate cheaply with a conditional request.
The HTTP header that tells browsers and CDNs whether and for how long a response may be cached (max-age, no-store, s-maxage, and so on).
Adding more CPU, memory or disk to a single machine; simple but bounded by hardware limits and a single point of failure.
Adding more machines and spreading load across them, which scales further and tolerates failures but requires distribution and coordination.
A service that keeps no per-client state between requests, so any instance can handle any request and instances are easy to add or replace.
Routing a client's requests to the same backend instance each time, usually because the instance holds session state.
Automatically adding or removing instances based on metrics such as CPU or queue depth, with cooldowns to avoid flapping.
A component that distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers and removes unhealthy ones from rotation.
Layer 4 balancers route by IP and port without reading the payload and are fast; layer 7 balancers inspect HTTP and can route by path, header or cookie.
A balancing algorithm that sends each new request to the next server in a fixed rotation, ignoring server load.
A balancing algorithm that sends each request to the server with the fewest active connections, adapting to uneven request cost.
A periodic probe that tells a load balancer or orchestrator whether an instance can serve traffic, so failed ones are removed.
Capping how many requests a client may make in a time window, protecting services from abuse and overload and answering with HTTP 429.
A rate-limiting algorithm in which tokens refill at a steady rate and each request spends one, allowing short bursts up to the bucket size.
A rate-limiting algorithm that queues requests and processes them at a constant rate, smoothing bursts into a steady flow.
A rate limiter that counts requests per fixed time interval; it is simple but permits a burst of up to twice the limit across a window boundary.
A rate limiter that weights the previous window's count by overlap with the current window to approximate a true sliding window cheaply.
Deliberately rejecting or dropping some requests when the system is overloaded so the rest are served within acceptable latency.
A signal from a slow consumer to its producers to slow down or stop, preventing unbounded queues and memory growth.
Isolating resources, such as separate thread pools or instances per dependency, so a failure or overload in one part cannot sink the whole system.
Continuing to provide reduced but useful functionality when a dependency fails or load is too high, instead of failing completely.
Estimating the resources needed to meet expected load with headroom, using traffic forecasts, per-instance throughput and failure margins.
The speedup from parallelizing a task is limited by its serial fraction: with serial fraction s, the maximum speedup is 1 divided by s.
